gettingStarted:
Install

npm install three-advanced-techniques

three.js is a peer dependency. Precomputed lighting also needs three-mesh-bvh.

Add a technique

Each technique is a TSL node or a class for WebGPURenderer. Bloom, on a scene you already render:

import * as THREE from 'three/webgpu'
import { pass } from 'three/tsl'
import { bloom } from 'three-advanced-techniques'

const scenePass = pass(scene, camera)
const sceneColor = scenePass.getTextureNode()
const bloomNode = bloom(sceneColor, { strength: 1, radius: 0.5, threshold: 0.8 })

const renderPipeline = new THREE.RenderPipeline(renderer)
renderPipeline.outputNode = sceneColor.add(bloomNode)

renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => renderPipeline.render())

Change options

Every option is also a property, so it can change while rendering:

bloomNode.strength = 2

The few that rebuild the node's shaders say so in their reference.

Import one module

Import a module by its path to load only that technique:

import { bloom } from 'three-advanced-techniques/rendering/bloom/BloomNode.js'

Without a bundler, map the packages in an import map, and pin each URL to a version in production:

<script type="importmap">
  {
    "imports": {
      "three": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three/build/three.webgpu.js",
      "three/webgpu": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three/build/three.webgpu.js",
      "three/tsl": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three/build/three.tsl.js",
      "three/addons/": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three/examples/jsm/",
      "three-advanced-techniques/": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three-advanced-techniques/"
    }
  }
</script>

Next

Each technique below has a guide and a live example. Each module has a reference of its classes, functions, options and types.

ambient-occlusion.title: Ambient Occlusion
ambient-occlusion.summary: A fast version of GTAO. XeGTAO's ground-truth ambient occlusion, at half resolution, denoised and accumulated over frames. Creases, contact and the gaps between things darken; open surfaces stay clean, with no noise left on them. After Intel's XeGTAO and Jimenez et al., Practical Real-Time Strategies for Accurate Indirect Occlusion (2016), accumulated as in Schied et al., Spatiotemporal Variance-Guided Filtering (2017).
ambient-occlusion.readme:
A fast version of GTAO. XeGTAO's ground-truth ambient occlusion, at half resolution, denoised and accumulated over frames. Creases, contact and the gaps between things darken; open surfaces stay clean, with no noise left on them. After Intel's XeGTAO and Jimenez et al., Practical Real-Time Strategies for Accurate Indirect Occlusion (2016), accumulated as in Schied et al., Spatiotemporal Variance-Guided Filtering (2017).

Usage

The occlusion runs on an opaque prepass's depth, and the scene's materials take it as their ambient occlusion: it darkens the ambient light only, not the direct light.

import * as THREE from 'three/webgpu'
import { builtinAOContext, context, pass } from 'three/tsl'
import { xeGTAO } from 'three-advanced-techniques'

const prePass = pass(scene, camera, { samples: 0 })
prePass.transparent = false
prePass.contextNode = context({ getAO: null }) // the prepass mustn't read the occlusion it feeds

const occlusion = xeGTAO(prePass.getTextureNode('depth'), camera, { radius: 0.5 }) // world units

const scenePass = pass(scene, camera)
scenePass.contextNode = builtinAOContext(occlusion.getMaterialAONode())

const renderPipeline = new THREE.RenderPipeline(renderer)
renderPipeline.outputNode = scenePass

Or, as a post effect on the scene pass's own depth, multiply its color by occlusion.getAONode(). That form can also take the scene pass's motion vectors as velocityNode, so what moves on its own reprojects along them. A normalNode, the view normal from the prepass, replaces the normals rebuilt from depth.

Why it's fast

Ambient occlusion reads the depth buffer many times per pixel, and cleaning up its noise reads the result many times again. This one keeps both cheap.

  • Half resolution, depth read once. It runs at half resolution, on a small copy of the depth made once per frame.
  • Few samples, no leftover noise. Each pixel searches only 2 directions, 3 steps each way, in a 4×4 pattern that a matching 4×4 blur averages back into a clean result. Only where something just moved, and there are no previous frames to blend with yet, does it search a third direction.
  • Two jobs in one pass. The blur and the blending with previous frames happen in the same pass.
  • A wider blur only where it's needed. Where something just moved, one more small pass blurs wider so the noise doesn't crawl; everywhere else it only copies the result through.
  • No full-size AO texture. The final upscale runs inside your materials' shader, and the background skips the search.

What it improves

  • Smooth, not grainy. The sampling pattern shifts every frame and the frames blend together, so the shading comes out smooth.
  • Shadows follow what moves. When an object moves, its darkening moves with it instead of smearing behind it.
  • Steady while things move. Around a moving object the sampling pattern holds still instead of shifting every frame, so what little noise is left doesn't flicker.
  • Clean outlines, near or far. The darkening stops at an object's outline, close up or far away, instead of spilling into a dark halo around it.
  • Lit areas stay bright. It dims only the soft ambient light, not direct light, so a crease in the sun doesn't turn grey.

area-light.title: Area Light
area-light.summary: Accurate soft shadows for three.js's RectAreaLight, ray-marched in screen space toward the light's whole area. Each pixel marches a fitted shadow map toward a few points on the emitter, after Xie, Tabellion and Pearce, Soft Shadows by Ray Tracing Multilayer Transparent Shadow Maps (2007), and the frames accumulate and filter in the order of Schied et al., Spatiotemporal Variance-Guided Filtering (2017). With it, rectAreaLTC gives three's rect-light shading, after Heitz et al., Real-Time Polygonal-Light Shading with Linearly Transformed Cosines (2016), as TSL helpers for custom lighting models.
area-light.readme:
Accurate soft shadows for three.js's RectAreaLight, ray-marched in screen space toward the light's whole area. Each pixel marches a fitted shadow map toward a few points on the emitter, after Xie, Tabellion and Pearce, Soft Shadows by Ray Tracing Multilayer Transparent Shadow Maps (2007), and the frames accumulate and filter in the order of Schied et al., Spatiotemporal Variance-Guided Filtering (2017). With it, rectAreaLTC gives three's rect-light shading, after Heitz et al., Real-Time Polygonal-Light Shading with Linearly Transformed Cosines (2016), as TSL helpers for custom lighting models.

Usage

npm install three three-advanced-techniques
import * as THREE from 'three/webgpu'
import { RectAreaLightShadow } from 'three-advanced-techniques' // also gives three's RectAreaLight its LTC tables

const light = new THREE.RectAreaLight('#fff0dc', 30, 1.2, 0.7) // a softbox overhead
light.position.set(0, 3.5, 0)
light.lookAt(0.3, 0, 0.3)
scene.add(light)
character.traverse((child) => (child.castShadow = true)) // receivers need a MeshStandardNodeMaterial or MeshPhysicalNodeMaterial

const shadow = new RectAreaLightShadow(light, {
  rayLength: 6, // metres the march reaches toward the light, 5 by default
})
await shadow.compileAsync(renderer, scene, camera)

renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => {
  mixer.update(delta) // every pose and transform first
  shadow.render(renderer, scene, camera) // then the mask, before the beauty
  renderer.render(scene, camera) // or renderPipeline.render()
})

The shadow takes over light.colorNode, multiplying the light by a screen-space mask, so it follows the light's color, intensity, width and height as they change. Call render() once a frame, outside any RenderPipeline; one shadow serves one light. getDebugNode('mask') shows the mask full-screen, and RectAreaLightShadowHelper draws the caster boxes and the fitted shadow camera.

For a lighting model of your own, rectAreaLTC splits three's rect-light maths into per-pixel and per-light helpers (ltcBasis, ltcLobe, rectAreaCorners, rectAreaDiffuseFormFactor, ltcFormFactor, ...), inlined with no WGSL functions, so several lights share one lobe lookup. horizonClip(builder, 'tabulated') adds Heitz's tabulated horizon clip, which is more accurate than three's analytic one near the horizon. In directRectArea(), the lightColor it hands you already carries the shadow.

Why it's fast

Soft shadows from an area light usually take many rays per pixel, or many shadow maps. This one takes a few per pixel per frame, and only where they can hit something.

  • Rays only where casters are. Each ray is clipped to the boxes of the casters it crosses, so a floor pixel beside a character marches that character's box alone, in short steps. Skinned characters are boxed by one box per bone, not by skinning their vertices on the CPU.
  • A shadow map fitted to the casters. The shadow camera wraps the casters every frame, so its texels go where the shadows are.
  • Half resolution. The march, its history and its blur run at half the screen's resolution, and the light reads the mask through a depth-aware upsample in its own shader: no extra full-screen pass.
  • Few samples, many frames. 4 points on the light and 10 steps per pixel per frame; the points move along a low-discrepancy sequence every frame and the history adds up to 16 frames.
  • One projection per ray. Each ray is projected into the shadow map once and interpolated there, not transformed at every step.

What it improves

  • No smearing behind moving casters. The history is shortened only where a moving caster's rays pass, by how fast it moves, so a running character's shadow keeps up while the still parts of the frame stay converged.
  • Its own motion vectors. It reprojects each surface by its own motion, skinning and instancing included, without touching three's velocity, so motion blur and TAAU keep theirs.

bloom.title: Bloom
bloom.summary: The classic mip-chain bloom of the Unreal Bloom, in 8 passes instead of 12, with its wide mips at a quarter of the usual pixels.
bloom.readme:
The classic mip-chain bloom of the Unreal Bloom, in 8 passes instead of 12, with its wide mips at a quarter of the usual pixels.

Usage

import * as THREE from 'three/webgpu'
import { pass } from 'three/tsl'
import { bloom } from 'three-advanced-techniques'

const scenePass = pass(scene, camera)
const sceneColor = scenePass.getTextureNode() // the input must be a texture node, such as a pass output

const bloomNode = bloom(sceneColor, { strength: 1, radius: 0.5, threshold: 0.8 })

const renderPipeline = new THREE.RenderPipeline(renderer)
renderPipeline.outputNode = sceneColor.add(bloomNode)

Why it's fast

Bloom's cost is memory traffic: every pass writes a texture and the next one reads it back. Fewer passes and smaller textures make it faster.

  • The threshold rides on the first blur, saving a whole pass and its texture.
  • One pass per mip. Only the first mip keeps the usual horizontal-then-vertical blur; each wider mip is a single small blur of the one before.
  • Smaller wide mips. The wide mips are so smooth they're stored at a quarter of the usual pixels.
  • Fewer texture reads. Where it can, two neighbouring blur weights share one filtered read.

What it improves

It looks the same as the classic bloom, the tight glow around bright spots and the wide, soft haze around it, only faster. Tint the glow with bloomTintColors, or choose what glows with highPassFn.

environment-lighting.title: Environment Lighting
environment-lighting.summary: Image-based lighting that keeps up with a changing scene. For the specular, SlicedPMREMGenerator regenerates a scene's PMREM a few cube faces or mip levels a frame. For the diffuse, IrradianceProbeColumn captures order-2 spherical-harmonic probes at a few heights on a vertical axis, projects them on the GPU and blends them by height. After Ramamoorthi and Hanrahan, An Efficient Representation for Irradiance Environment Maps (2001), Sloan, Stupid Spherical Harmonics (SH) Tricks (2008), and Driscoll, Cubemap Texel Solid Angle (2012).
environment-lighting.readme:
Image-based lighting that keeps up with a changing scene. For the specular, SlicedPMREMGenerator regenerates a scene's PMREM a few cube faces or mip levels a frame. For the diffuse, IrradianceProbeColumn captures order-2 spherical-harmonic probes at a few heights on a vertical axis, projects them on the GPU and blends them by height. After Ramamoorthi and Hanrahan, An Efficient Representation for Irradiance Environment Maps (2001), Sloan, Stupid Spherical Harmonics (SH) Tricks (2008), and Driscoll, Cubemap Texel Solid Angle (2012).

Usage

npm install three three-advanced-techniques
import * as THREE from 'three/webgpu'
import { IrradianceProbeColumn, SlicedPMREMGenerator } from 'three-advanced-techniques'

// Captured from inside the object, without it
object.visible = false

// The specular: the scene's PMREM
const generator = new SlicedPMREMGenerator(renderer) // samples: 32 for a faster prefilter, null for three's
const capture = { near: 0.05, far: 20, size: 256, position: new THREE.Vector3(0, 1, 0) }
const pmrem = generator.fromScene(scene, 0, capture.near, capture.far, capture)
material.envMap = pmrem.texture

// The diffuse: probes on the object's vertical axis, at heights along the column's +y
const probes = new IrradianceProbeColumn([0.3, 1, 1.7], { near: capture.near, far: capture.far })
probes.update(renderer, scene)
material.contextNode = probes.irradianceContext

object.visible = true

// While the scene changes: one slice a frame, then a swap the materials don't notice
let job = null
renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => {
  renderer.render(scene, camera)
  object.visible = false
  job ??= generator.fromSceneSliced(scene, { ...capture, facesPerSlice: 2 })
  if (job.step()) {
    job.copyTo(pmrem) // texel for texel, into the texture the materials read
    probes.update(renderer, scene) // or sliced too: probes.capture(renderer, scene, i, { faces: [0, 3] }), then probes.project(renderer)
    job = null
  }
  object.visible = true
})

The column is an Object3D: move it onto the object's axis, and an object turning about that axis keeps the same probes. irradianceContext changes standard and physical materials lit by an environment (envMap, envNode or scene.environment) on the WebGPU backend. IrradianceProbeColumnHelper shows each probe as a sphere lit by it alone.

Why it's fast

Regenerating an environment means rendering the scene six times and prefiltering the result, which is a hitch when it lands in one frame. These spread it out and keep it on the GPU.

  • No hitch. A PMREM is 6 face renders and a prefilter pass per mip level; the job runs a few of them a frame into a back target.
  • A prefilter in one pass. three's prefilter renders each face of each mip level in a pass of its own, 36 at 256², with 256 GGX samples a texel on the sharp levels, and those passes cost more than the sampling. SlicedPMREMGenerator renders every level into one atlas in one pass, with 64 filtered importance samples a texel on level 1, doubling each level, and copies the atlas into the PMREM in one command buffer: 0.43 ms against 4.47 on a Mac mini, with an error against a 4096-sample reference a little above three's.
  • No rebinding. The finished PMREM is copied into the live texture level by level, so materials keep their texture and nothing recompiles.
  • Projected on the GPU. Compute passes reduce each probe's cube to its 9 coefficients, which stay in a storage buffer the fragments read: no readback, no frame of latency.
  • Small captures. 9 coefficients keep only the low frequencies, so a 64×64 cube per probe is plenty; the demo takes 128×128 so its thin neon tubes don't fall between texels.
  • Cheap to shade. A fragment blends two probes' 9 coefficients in a few dozen multiply-adds, or a vertex does it with perVertex.

What it improves

  • Diffuse that changes with height. A PMREM is seen from one point; the probes see the floor's bounce at the feet and the ceiling's light at the head.
  • The right lobe. The PMREM's roughest level is broader than the cosine lobe the diffuse needs, which flattens the shading; 9 SH coefficients give the cosine-weighted irradiance to within a few percent. windowing damps the ringing of small bright lights.

motion-blur.title: Motion Blur
motion-blur.summary: Object and camera motion blur as a tile-based reconstruction filter, after McGuire et al., A Reconstruction Filter for Plausible Motion Blur (2012), Guertin et al., A Fast and Stable Feature-Aware Motion Blur Filter (2014), Jimenez, Next Generation Post Processing in Call of Duty: Advanced Warfare (2014).
motion-blur.readme:
Object and camera motion blur as a tile-based reconstruction filter, after McGuire et al., A Reconstruction Filter for Plausible Motion Blur (2012), Guertin et al., A Fast and Stable Feature-Aware Motion Blur Filter (2014), Jimenez, Next Generation Post Processing in Call of Duty: Advanced Warfare (2014).

Usage

import * as THREE from 'three/webgpu'
import { mrt, output, pass, velocity } from 'three/tsl'
import { motionBlur } from 'three-advanced-techniques'

const scenePass = pass(scene, camera)
scenePass.setMRT(mrt({ output, velocity }))
const velocityTexture = scenePass.getTexture('velocity')
velocityTexture.type = THREE.HalfFloatType // RG16F
velocityTexture.format = THREE.RGFormat

const blurred = motionBlur(scenePass.getTextureNode('output'), scenePass.getTextureNode('depth'), camera, {
  velocityNode: scenePass.getTextureNode('velocity'), // omit for camera motion only, without the MRT
  shutterAngle: 180,
})

const renderPipeline = new THREE.RenderPipeline(renderer)
renderPipeline.outputNode = blurred

Why it's fast

A simple motion blur takes 16 samples along every pixel's motion, even where nothing moves. This one spends samples only where there's motion to show.

  • Still areas are free. A quick compute pass finds the largest motion in each 32×32-pixel tile; pixels with no motion nearby are left as they are.
  • Uniform motion gets a cheap blur. Where everything moves together a plain blur is enough; only the edges between different motions pay for the full depth-aware one.
  • Samples scale with the streak. One sample every 2 pixels, up to 16, so short streaks are cheap.
  • Small inputs, no extra pass. Velocity and depth are packed into a quarter-size texture, and the blur runs inside the pass that uses it.
  • Camera-only motion needs no velocity buffer. Camera motion is worked out from depth.

What it improves

It reduces glitches and visual errors:

  • Streaks past the outline. Each pixel blurs along its neighbourhood's largest motion, so a moving object's streak reaches past its silhouette.
  • No bleeding between depths. Taps are weighted by depth, so near and far objects don't smear into each other.
  • No stepped copies. Taps are jittered, so a streak reads as a smooth blur, not repeated copies of the object.
  • Steady through hitches. Streak length follows a smoothed frame time, so a slow frame doesn't flash a long streak.

precomputed-lighting.title: Precomputed Lighting
precomputed-lighting.summary: Self-shadows, bounce light and soft contact shadows for a rigid mesh, precomputed once and shaded live as the mesh turns and the lights move. SelfShadowVisibilityMasks stores, per vertex, the directions that escape the mesh as a bit mask; SelfShadowRadianceTransfer stores them as 16 spherical-harmonic coefficients, for softer shadows. PrecomputedRadiosity adds the light the mesh bounces onto itself, as Enlighten does. PrecomputedAmbientOcclusion bakes ambient occlusion and a rect light's soft shadow onto static surfaces, and ContactOcclusion darkens the floor under objects as they move. After Sloan et al., Precomputed Radiance Transfer (2002), Hanrahan et al., A Rapid Hierarchical Radiosity Algorithm (1991), Martin and Einarsson, A Real-Time Radiosity Architecture for Video Games (2010), and Heitz et al., Combining Analytic Direct Illumination and Stochastic Shadows (2018).
precomputed-lighting.readme:
Self-shadows, bounce light and soft contact shadows for a rigid mesh, precomputed once and shaded live as the mesh turns and the lights move. SelfShadowVisibilityMasks stores, per vertex, the directions that escape the mesh as a bit mask; SelfShadowRadianceTransfer stores them as 16 spherical-harmonic coefficients, for softer shadows. PrecomputedRadiosity adds the light the mesh bounces onto itself, as Enlighten does. PrecomputedAmbientOcclusion bakes ambient occlusion and a rect light's soft shadow onto static surfaces, and ContactOcclusion darkens the floor under objects as they move. After Sloan et al., Precomputed Radiance Transfer (2002), Hanrahan et al., A Rapid Hierarchical Radiosity Algorithm (1991), Martin and Einarsson, A Real-Time Radiosity Architecture for Video Games (2010), and Heitz et al., Combining Analytic Direct Illumination and Stochastic Shadows (2018).

Usage

Make sure to install three-mesh-bvh as well, needed by every class here to build the BVH their bakes trace rays against:

npm install three three-mesh-bvh three-advanced-techniques

SelfShadowVisibilityMasks

import * as THREE from 'three/webgpu'
import { attribute } from 'three/tsl'
import { SelfShadowVisibilityMasks } from 'three-advanced-techniques'

// The mesh's geometry needs an index and normals; up to four lights of any kind
const masks = new SelfShadowVisibilityMasks(mesh, [keyLight, rimLight, sun, sky], { softness: 0.01 }) // σ in mesh units
await masks.bake(renderer, { resolution: 64 }) // kept as masks.data, plain typed arrays: cache them
// Optional: while a light moves in the mesh's frame, spread by one gather over pairs of vertices instead of the
// explicit steps; built in workers for that σ alone, structured-cloneable to cache
masks.motionKernel = await masks.diffusion.createKernel(masks.softness, { clusterSize: 2, mass: 0.99 })
await masks.compileAsync(renderer) // optional: every pipeline update() may build, ahead
mesh.geometry.setAttribute('visibility', masks.visibility) // per vertex: light 0's visibility in x, light 1's in y, …

// Each direct light's contribution × its visibility: the rect lights', and the directional, point and spot lights'
const selfShadow = attribute('visibility', 'vec4')
const visibleFrom = (light) => selfShadow[{ [keyLight.id]: 'x', [rimLight.id]: 'y', [sun.id]: 'z' }[light.id]].saturate()
class MaskedLighting extends THREE.PhysicalLightingModel {
  directRectArea(input, builder) {
    super.directRectArea({ ...input, lightColor: input.lightColor.mul(visibleFrom(input.lightNode.light)) }, builder)
  }
  direct(input, builder) {
    super.direct({ ...input, lightColor: input.lightColor.mul(visibleFrom(input.lightNode.light)) }, builder)
  }
}
mesh.material.setupLightingModel = () => new MaskedLighting()
// An ambient or hemisphere light's or a probe's visibility is the occlusion of that sky: it scales the indirect light
mesh.material.aoNode = selfShadow.w.saturate()

renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => {
  masks.update(renderer) // evaluates only the lights that moved in the mesh's frame
  renderer.render(scene, camera)
})

SelfShadowRadianceTransfer

import { SelfShadowRadianceTransfer } from 'three-advanced-techniques'

// The same self-shadow in order-4 spherical harmonics, with the same API: softer, with no crisp shadow

screen-space-reflections.title: Screen-Space Reflections
screen-space-reflections.summary: Cheap Screen-space Reflections found by Newton's method on the depth buffer instead of a ray march, after Mayer, Assarsson and Sintorn, Ultrafast Screen-Space Refractions and Caustics via Newton's Method (2026).
screen-space-reflections.readme:
Cheap Screen-space Reflections found by Newton's method on the depth buffer instead of a ray march, after Mayer, Assarsson and Sintorn, Ultrafast Screen-Space Refractions and Caustics via Newton's Method (2026).

Usage

import * as THREE from 'three/webgpu'
import { mrt, output, pass, rtt, velocity } from 'three/tsl'
import { traa } from 'three/addons/tsl/display/TRAANode.js'
import { ssr, ssrComposite, ssrGBuffer } from 'three-advanced-techniques'

const scenePass = pass(scene, camera, { samples: 0 })
scenePass.setMRT(mrt({ output, velocity, ...ssrGBuffer() }))
const velocityTexture = scenePass.getTexture('velocity')
velocityTexture.type = THREE.HalfFloatType // RG16F
velocityTexture.format = THREE.RGFormat

const color = scenePass.getTextureNode()
const reflections = ssr(color, scenePass, { roughnessCutoff: 0.6, thickness: 0.2 })
const composite = ssrComposite(color, reflections, scene.environment, {
  environmentIntensity: () => scene.environmentIntensity,
  environmentRotation: scene.environmentRotation,
})

const renderPipeline = new THREE.RenderPipeline(renderer)
renderPipeline.outputNode = traa(
  rtt(composite, null, null, { type: THREE.HalfFloatType }),
  scenePass.getTextureNode('depth'),
  scenePass.getTextureNode('velocity'),
  camera,
)

Why it's fast

The usual ray march steps along each reflected ray, reading the depth buffer every pixel or two until it hits something: hundreds of reads for a long reflection. This one needs a few.

  • A few jumps instead of many steps. Newton's method jumps straight to where the ray meets the surface below it: one jump on a flat floor, a few on a curved one, however long the reflection.
  • Last frame's answer first. Each pixel starts from where its reflection landed last frame, so a reflection that hasn't changed is only checked, not searched for.
  • It skips what you won't see. Pixels too rough or too faint to reflect take the environment map instead.
  • Optional half resolution. resolutionScale: 0.5 traces a quarter of the pixels.

What it improves

  • Sharp on smooth surfaces, blurry on rough ones. A polished floor shows a crisp mirror image, a rougher one a soft, spread-out reflection.
  • Strongest at grazing angles. Surfaces reflect more as you look across them and less as you look straight down, like real materials, and replace the environment's reflection instead of adding to it, so they don't get too bright.
  • No ghost reflections. Each hit is checked against the surface it lands on, so nothing shows up in a reflection where it isn't.
  • No hard edges. Reflections of what's off screen fade smoothly into the environment instead of cutting off.

taau.title: TAAU
taau.summary: Temporal anti-aliasing upscaling: the scene renders jittered, at or below the output's resolution, and each frame joins the history into one stable, anti-aliased image at the output's. Thin features stay locked, edges stay smooth. After Karis, High Quality Temporal Supersampling (2014), and AMD's FidelityFX Super Resolution 2 (2022).
taau.readme:
Temporal anti-aliasing upscaling: the scene renders jittered, at or below the output's resolution, and each frame joins the history into one stable, anti-aliased image at the output's. Thin features stay locked, edges stay smooth. After Karis, High Quality Temporal Supersampling (2014), and AMD's FidelityFX Super Resolution 2 (2022).

Usage

npm install three three-advanced-techniques
import * as THREE from 'three/webgpu'
import { mrt, output, pass, renderOutput, velocity } from 'three/tsl'
import { taau } from 'three-advanced-techniques'

const scenePass = pass(scene, camera, { samples: 0 }) // no MSAA
scenePass.setMRT(mrt({ output, velocity }))
scenePass.setResolutionScale(0.5) // input / output: 1 anti-aliases at full resolution
const depth = scenePass.getTextureNode('depth')
const taauNode = taau(scenePass.getTextureNode('output'), depth, scenePass.getTextureNode('velocity'), camera, {
  maxAccumulation: 24, // samples a pixel accumulates, 16 by default
})

const renderPipeline = new THREE.RenderPipeline(renderer)
renderPipeline.outputColorTransform = false
renderPipeline.outputNode = renderOutput(taauNode.getTextureNode())

The camera is jittered only while the pipeline renders, so picking and the shadow maps see it still. Read the output through getTextureNode(): it ping-pongs. If TAAU can leave the output graph, call syncUnjitteredProjection(camera) once a frame before rendering: the scene's velocity keeps reading the projection TAAU handed it.

Why it's fast

Upscaling is limited by memory traffic: every pass reads its inputs and the previous frame, and writes full-size textures. This one keeps that traffic down.

  • Shared work. What the output needs from each low-resolution pixel is worked out once and shared by the output pixels over it, four at a 2× upscale.
  • Fewer reads. The reconstruction takes 4 filtered reads instead of 9.
  • No copies. The output alternates between two history textures, so nothing is copied into a third.
  • Small textures. Its per-pixel bookkeeping is packed into compact formats.

What it improves

It reduces ghosting and blur:

  • Sharp, not soft. Past frames are resampled with a sharp filter, so detail doesn't soften frame after frame.
  • No ghost trails. Past frames only keep colours the current frame has nearby, and are dropped where depth jumps, so moving objects don't leave trails behind.
  • Thin details hold still. Wires, railings and other lines under two pixels wide stay steady instead of flickering or breaking up.
  • Smooth edges in motion. An object's outline stays anti-aliased as it moves, instead of turning jagged over the background it uncovers.

noodles.title: Noodles
noodles.summary: Compute shader strand simulation in TSL. NoodleSimulation simulates noodles, ropes and cables that bend, buckle, pile up and never pass through each other. WormSimulation builds soft, crawling worms on it.
noodles.readme:
Compute shader strand simulation in TSL. NoodleSimulation simulates noodles, ropes and cables that bend, buckle, pile up and never pass through each other. WormSimulation builds soft, crawling worms on it.

NoodleSimulation

Each noodle is a chain of particles joined by capsules, simulated in small fixed time steps so it moves the same at any frame rate. After Macklin et al., XPBD: Position-Based Simulation of Compliant Constrained Dynamics (2016), Han and Harada, Tridiagonal Matrix Formulation for Inextensible Hair Strand Simulation (2013), Bergou et al., Discrete Elastic Rods (2008), Ericson, Real-Time Collision Detection (2005), Tonge et al., Mass Splitting for Jitter-Free Parallel Rigid Body Simulation (2012), Wu et al., A Safe and Fast Repulsion Method for GPU-based Cloth Self Collisions (2020), and Chen et al., Offset Geometric Contact (2025).

Usage

import * as THREE from 'three/webgpu'
import { NoodleSimulation } from 'three-advanced-techniques'

// one curve per noodle: its rest shape and starting pose
const curves = points.map((p) => new THREE.LineCurve3(p, p.clone().add(new THREE.Vector3(0, -3, 0))))
const noodles = new NoodleSimulation(curves, material, { radius: 0.05, particlesPerNoodle: 32 })
noodles.bendingCompliance = 0.5 // stiffer
noodles.bendingPlasticity = 0 // ropes and cables spring back
noodles.colliders.push(new THREE.Sphere(center, 0.5))
scene.add(noodles)

const timer = new THREE.Timer()
renderer.setAnimationLoop((time) => {
  timer.update(time)
  noodles.update(renderer, timer.getDelta())
  renderer.render(scene, camera)
})

How it works

  • Bending: each noodle bends like a soft rod, solved on the GPU one noodle per workgroup. bendingCompliance sets how floppy it is, whatever its particle count: 2 is cooked spaghetti, 0.08 a stiff rod. bendingPlasticity lets a noodle keep the shape it settles in; at 0 it springs back.
  • Length: each noodle's length is solved exactly in one step, so it never stretches. It squashes a little more easily, so a noodle landing on its end buckles.
  • Contacts: segments are sorted into a grid, so each one only tests its neighbours, and overlapping noodles are pushed apart with friction.
  • No passing through: with strictCollisions, a particle never moves more than about half its distance to the nearest other segment in one step, so noodles can't pass through each other.
  • Colliders: a ground plane plus planes, spheres, boxes and capsules you can move every frame. Add another NoodleSimulation to colliders and the two collide.
  • Drawing: every noodle is drawn as a tube in one draw call, with any material.
  • Extending it: extraPasses runs your own compute shaders on its data, and pickAsync, startGrab, moveGrab and endGrab let you drag a noodle.

WormSimulation

Worms are noodles that move themselves: they only add pushes and muscle bends, so the noodle physics, length, bending and collisions, always wins. Everything runs on the GPU, and nothing is read back to the CPU.

Usage

import * as THREE from 'three/webgpu'
import { WormSimulation } from 'three-advanced-techniques'
import { BodyField } from './BodyField.js' // copied from the repo's examples/utils, not in the package

const field = BodyField.fromSkinnedMesh(body) // the body the worms climb: round cones on its bones
const worms = new WormSimulation(curves, material, { field, radius: 0.024, particlesPerNoodle: 18 })
worms.colliders.push(...field.colliders)
scene.add(worms)

const timer = new THREE.Timer()
renderer.setAnimationLoop((time) => {
  timer.update(time)
  const dt = timer.getDelta()
  field.update(dt)
  worms.update(renderer, dt)
  renderer.render(scene, camera)
})

worms.poke(raycaster) // knock worms off along a ray

How it works

  • Crawling: muscles bend each worm in a travelling wave, like a snake. Worms also steer and squirm, and can squeeze along their length (peristalsis).
  • States: each worm is loose, crawling, climbing or held, and can switch once a frame.
  • Body: the worms climb a shape given as a distance field: how far each point is from its surface, which way is out, and how fast it moves. Inside it, worms are nearly weightless and fill it from the bottom up; those that don't fit drip off and crawl back.
  • Floor grip: worms stick to the floor and slide more easily forward than sideways, so the wave moves them forward.
  • Tools: poke, blast, strike and collapse knock worms off; pick, grabPicked and moveGrabAlongRay drag one; reset({ clock: true }) replays a run.

reaction-diffusion.title: Reaction Diffusion
reaction-diffusion.summary: Compute shader reaction-diffusion in TSL. ReactionDiffusionSimulation2D grows Gray-Scott patterns over the surface of any triangle mesh and draws that mesh raised where the pattern grows, with any material. After Turk, Generating Textures on Arbitrary Surfaces Using Reaction-Diffusion (1991), Pearson, Complex Patterns in a Simple System (1993), and Sims, Reaction-Diffusion Tutorial.
reaction-diffusion.readme:
Compute shader reaction-diffusion in TSL. ReactionDiffusionSimulation2D grows Gray-Scott patterns over the surface of any triangle mesh and draws that mesh raised where the pattern grows, with any material. After Turk, Generating Textures on Arbitrary Surfaces Using Reaction-Diffusion (1991), Pearson, Complex Patterns in a Simple System (1993), and Sims, Reaction-Diffusion Tutorial.

Usage

npm install three three-advanced-techniques
import * as THREE from 'three/webgpu'
import { color, mix } from 'three/tsl'
import { ReactionDiffusionSimulation2D } from 'three-advanced-techniques'

// The pattern is a few edges wide: a finer mesh grows a finer pattern.
const geometry = new THREE.IcosahedronGeometry(1, 63)
const reactionDiffusion = new ReactionDiffusionSimulation2D(geometry, new THREE.MeshStandardNodeMaterial(), {
  feedRate: 0.0545, // coral
  killRate: 0.062,
  displacementAmplitude: 0.02, // how far the ridges rise
})
// 0 in the grooves, 1 on the ridges
reactionDiffusion.material.colorNode = mix(color('#1d2230'), color('#e0b25a'), reactionDiffusion.smoothPatternNode)
scene.add(reactionDiffusion)
await reactionDiffusion.compileAsync(renderer)

const timer = new THREE.Timer()
renderer.setAnimationLoop((time) => {
  timer.update(time)
  reactionDiffusion.brush = raycaster.intersectObject(reactionDiffusion)[0]?.point ?? null // while dragging: a point or a THREE.Line3, world space
  reactionDiffusion.update(renderer, timer.getDelta())
  renderer.render(scene, camera)
})

reset() starts over from scattered seeds, and clear() empties the surface for the brush to seed (brushMode = 'seed') or carve ('erase'). Every option is a live property: rd.feedRate = 0.0367 and rd.killRate = 0.0649 turn the coral into dividing spots.

How it works

  • Any mesh. The two chemicals live on the vertices, welded by position, so the pattern flows across UV and hard-normal seams. Each vertex diffuses toward the mean of its neighbours, so lengths are counted in edges: an even mesh, such as an icosphere or a remesh, grows an even pattern.
  • Relief. The pattern raises the surface along its normals, and the normals tilt with the pattern's slope, so any material shades the relief, shadows included. smoothPatternNode bends the pattern's contours across each triangle, smooth on a coarse mesh.
  • Brush. A point or a THREE.Line3 stroke, in world space, seeds or erases the vertices within brushRadius on every update while it's set. Below 1, brushStrength blends toward that instead, so a stroke can fade out.

Why it's fast

  • Only what changes is simulated. Vertices are stepped in blocks of 64 nearby ones. A block sleeps while neither it nor a block next to it changed, as ahead of a growth front; with a small sleepThreshold, such as 1e-6, a pattern that has nearly settled sleeps too. The GPU lists the awake blocks and dispatches only those, nothing read back.
  • Neighbours from workgroup memory. Each block loads its vertices and the ring around them into workgroup memory once, and every vertex reads its neighbours from there, their indices packed 8 or 16 bits each.
  • One dispatch list a frame. A frame's steps, the brush and the surface refresh go out in one renderer.compute(), ping-ponging between two buffers.
  • A cheap draw. The pattern and its slope are computed once per vertex per frame, only where it changed; the vertex shader reads them, displaces and tilts the normal, with no normals recomputed.

import * as THREE from 'three/webgpu'
import { color, mix } from 'three/tsl'
import { ReactionDiffusionSimulation2D } from 'three-advanced-techniques'

// The pattern is a few edges wide: a finer mesh grows a finer pattern.
const geometry = new THREE.IcosahedronGeometry(1, 63)
const reactionDiffusion = new ReactionDiffusionSimulation2D(geometry, new THREE.MeshStandardNodeMaterial(), {
  feedRate: 0.0545, // coral
  killRate: 0.062,
  displacementAmplitude: 0.02, // how far the ridges rise
})
// 0 in the grooves, 1 on the ridges
reactionDiffusion.material.colorNode = mix(color('#1d2230'), color('#e0b25a'), reactionDiffusion.smoothPatternNode)
scene.add(reactionDiffusion)
await reactionDiffusion.compileAsync(renderer)

const timer = new THREE.Timer()
renderer.setAnimationLoop((time) => {
  timer.update(time)
  reactionDiffusion.brush = raycaster.intersectObject(reactionDiffusion)[0]?.point ?? null // while dragging: a point or a THREE.Line3, world space
  reactionDiffusion.update(renderer, timer.getDelta())
  renderer.render(scene, camera)
})

reset() starts over from scattered seeds, and clear() empties the surface for the brush to seed (brushMode = 'seed') or carve ('erase'). Every option is a live property: rd.feedRate = 0.0367 and rd.killRate = 0.0649 turn the coral into dividing spots.

gpu-tier-detector.title: GPU Tier Detector
gpu-tier-detector.summary: Picks a quality tier for the device at load.
gpu-tier-detector.readme:
Picks a quality tier for the device at load: a classification from the adapter's static signals (vendor, architecture, limits, navigator.userAgentData), then optionally a short GPU benchmark. Plain WebGPU, no three.js needed: it runs before any renderer exists, or reads one's.

import { GPUTierDetector } from 'three-advanced-techniques/utils/GPUTierDetector.js'

const detector = new GPUTierDetector(['Low', 'Medium', 'High'], { caps: { mobile: 'Low', desktop: 'Medium' } })
const found = await detector.detect() // an adapter of its own, a few ms
// { tier: 'Low', level: 0, deviceClass: 'mobile', mobile: true, reasons: ['apple GPU on a mobile device'], … }
// or detect(renderer) after `await renderer.init()`, detect(device) or detect(adapter)

// optionally, time one unit of the app's GPU work (or omit it for a built-in reference set)
const timed = await detector.benchmark(renderer, () => app.simulate(renderer, 1 / 60))
// { tier: 'Medium', level: 1, ms: 11.4, samples: [11.2, 11.4, 11.9], roundTrip: 0.04, warmups: 3, … }
const capped = detector.tiers[Math.min(found.level, timed.level)]

detect() sorts the device into a class, fallback, weak, mobile or desktop, and caps the tier at the class's highest (caps); its mobile is true for a phone or a tablet by navigator.userAgentData (mobile, or a formFactors hint of Mobile, Tablet, XR or Watch), else by the user-agent string and touch points (Safari, Firefox), or for a mobile vendor's GPU outside Windows (an Android tablet asking for desktop sites, a Chromebook), whatever the class.

benchmark() times workload as wall time from the call to device.queue.onSubmittedWorkDone(), minus an empty submit's round trip, and picks the highest tier whose threshold the median meets. Pass-timestamp sums are never used: on Vulkan a pass's begin stamp can absorb the wait for earlier work. Compile the workload's pipelines before benchmark(), or the warm-up run carries the compile. It times the whole device queue: stop anything else that submits while it runs (renderer.setAnimationLoop(null), or skip the loop's render), or its frames land in the samples. Without workload it times a built-in reference set of compute dispatches, on the given device or, with none, on a device of its own.

Options and properties

  • tiers: The tier names, lowest first (positional).
  • thresholds: ms of one workload unit at most for each tier above the lowest, in tier order (tiers.length − 1 values). Default: provisional values for the built-in workload.
  • caps: { fallback, weak, mobile, desktop }: the highest tier of each device class, as names or levels. Default { fallback: lowest, weak: lowest, mobile: tiers.length − 2, desktop: highest }.
  • warmups: Untimed runs before the samples, at least.
  • warmupTime: ms: the warm-up runs on until this much has passed (GPU clocks ramp up under load), within half the budget.
  • samples: Timed runs; the result is their median.
  • abortTime: ms: a sample over it ends the benchmark at the lowest tier.
  • budget: ms for the whole benchmark; once spent, it stops after the current sample (one sample at least).
  • penalties: deviceMemory ≤ 4 GB and hardwareConcurrency ≤ 4 (not on WebKit) each move the class one down.
gpu-tier-detector.usage:
import { GPUTierDetector } from 'three-advanced-techniques/utils/GPUTierDetector.js'

const detector = new GPUTierDetector(['Low', 'Medium', 'High'], { caps: { mobile: 'Low', desktop: 'Medium' } })
const found = await detector.detect() // an adapter of its own, a few ms
// { tier: 'Low', level: 0, deviceClass: 'mobile', mobile: true, reasons: ['apple GPU on a mobile device'], … }
// or detect(renderer) after `await renderer.init()`, detect(device) or detect(adapter)

// optionally, time one unit of the app's GPU work (or omit it for a built-in reference set)
const timed = await detector.benchmark(renderer, () => app.simulate(renderer, 1 / 60))
// { tier: 'Medium', level: 1, ms: 11.4, samples: [11.2, 11.4, 11.9], roundTrip: 0.04, warmups: 3, … }
const capped = detector.tiers[Math.min(found.level, timed.level)]

XeGTAONode.summary: XeGTAO ambient occlusion at a fraction of the resolution, denoised and accumulated over frames.
XeGTAONode.intro: XeGTAO ambient occlusion at a fraction of the resolution, denoised and accumulated over frames. On the ambient light alone, from an opaque prepass's depth:
XeGTAONode.usage:
prePass.contextNode = context({ getAO: null }) // the prepass mustn't read the AO it feeds
const occlusion = xeGTAO(prePass.getTextureNode('depth'), camera, { radius: 0.5 }) // world units
scenePass.contextNode = builtinAOContext(occlusion.getMaterialAONode())
await occlusion.compileAsync(renderer) // optional: compiles its passes ahead of the first frame
XeGTAONode.outro: Or as a post effect: multiply the scene's color by occlusion.getAONode().

const shadow = new RectAreaLightShadow(rectAreaLight, { rayLength: 5 })

  renderer.render(scene, camera)

rectAreaLTC.summary: three's RectAreaLight shading (linearly transformed cosines) as plain TSL helpers, the per-pixel work split from the per-light work so several lights share it.
rectAreaLTC.intro: three's RectAreaLight shading (linearly transformed cosines) as plain TSL helpers, the per-pixel work split from the per-light work so several lights share it. Importing it also gives three's RectAreaLight its LTC tables, built when the first shader reads them, in place of RectAreaLightNode.setLTC():
rectAreaLTC.usage:
// in a PhysicalLightingModel subclass's directRectArea({ lightPosition, halfWidth, halfHeight, ... }, builder)
const lobe = ltcLobe(builder, { basis: ltcBasis(normalView, positionViewDirection), roughness, f0, f90 })
const clip = horizonClip(builder, 'tabulated')
If(rectAreaFacing(lightPosition.sub(positionView), halfWidth, halfHeight), () => {
  const corners = rectAreaCorners(lightPosition, positionView, halfWidth, halfHeight)
  diffuse.assign(rectAreaDiffuseFormFactor(corners, normalView, clip)) // × colour × diffuse albedo
  specular.assign(ltcFormFactor(corners, lobe, clip)) // × colour × lobe.fresnel
})

SlicedPMREMGenerator.summary: three's PMREMGenerator.fromScene() spread over several calls, so a scene's PMREM regenerates over frames, with a faster prefilter.
SlicedPMREMGenerator.intro: three's PMREMGenerator.fromScene() spread over several calls, so a scene's PMREM regenerates over frames, with a faster prefilter: one pass for every mip level where three's takes one per face and level:
SlicedPMREMGenerator.usage:
const generator = new SlicedPMREMGenerator(renderer) // generator.samples = null for three's prefilter
const live = generator.fromScene(scene, 0, 0.05, 30, { size: 256, position })
scene.environment = live.texture

let job = generator.fromSceneSliced(scene, { near: 0.05, far: 30, size: 256, position })
// once a frame
if (job !== null && job.step()) {
  job.copyTo(live) // texel-exact: materials keep their texture
  job = null
}

ContactOcclusion.summary: The contact occlusion objects cast on a horizontal floor about them, baked once into a square texture in another object's frame, so it turns and moves with that object.
ContactOcclusion.intro: The contact occlusion objects cast on a horizontal floor about them, baked once into a square texture in another object's frame, so it turns and moves with that object:
ContactOcclusion.usage:
const contact = new ContactOcclusion(turntable, { size: 2.4, resolution: 128, height: 0.001 })
floor.material.aoNode = contact.aoNode
await contact.bake(baker, { rays: 128, maxDistance: 0.6 }) // a PrecomputedAmbientOcclusion of the occluders
ContactOcclusion.guide:
UUnlike the classic ContactShadow, which render the objects' silhouette from below and blur it every frame, ContactOcclusion ray traces the floor's ambient occlusion once, so a frame costs one texture read, but it holds only while the objects keep their pose in the frame.

import { ContactOcclusion, PrecomputedAmbientOcclusion } from 'three-advanced-techniques'

// The contact occlusion on the floor about the objects, in a texture in the turntable's frame, so it turns with it

PrecomputedAmbientOcclusion.intro: The ambient occlusion static occluder meshes cast at static receiver points, and any light's soft shadow and the thickness there, ray traced on the CPU in persistent workers against a BVH of the occluders:

const baker = new PrecomputedAmbientOcclusion(sculpture) // captured in world space now
const visibility = await baker.bakeVisibility(rectAreaLight, receivers, { samples: 8 })

import * as THREE from 'three/webgpu'

const receivers = pedestal.geometry.clone().applyMatrix4(pedestal.matrixWorld)
const occlusion = await baker.bakeOcclusion(receivers, { rays: 64, maxDistance: 0.5 }) // Float32Array, 0 … 1
pedestal.geometry.setAttribute('occlusion', new THREE.BufferAttribute(occlusion, 1))
pedestal.material.aoNode = attribute('occlusion', 'float')

PrecomputedRadiosity.summary: The diffuse interreflection within one rigid mesh, precomputed as Enlighten does.
PrecomputedRadiosity.intro: The diffuse interreflection within one rigid mesh, precomputed as Enlighten does: the light transport between the mesh's own surfaces is baked once from the geometry, and the bounce under any lighting is a few sparse gathers on the GPU:
PrecomputedRadiosity.usage:
const radiosity = new PrecomputedRadiosity(mesh, { lights: [rectAreaLight], albedo: 0xe7e7e7, bounces: 2 })
const transfer = await radiosity.bake({ rays: 256, patches: 4096 }) // in workers; cache it, or setTransfer() it
material.emissiveNode = diffuseColor.rgb.mul(radiosity.irradianceNode).div(Math.PI)
renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => {
  radiosity.update(renderer) // recomputes only when an input changed
  renderer.render(scene, camera)
})
PrecomputedRadiosity.guide:
import { diffuseColor } from 'three/tsl'
import { PrecomputedRadiosity } from 'three-advanced-techniques'

// The light the mesh bounces onto itself, from any of three's lights, unoccluded
const radiosity = new PrecomputedRadiosity(mesh, { lights: [keyLight], albedo: 0xe9e3d9, bounces: 2 })
await radiosity.bake({ rays: 128, patches: 2048 }) // in workers; resolves to a transfer to cache
mesh.material.emissiveNode = diffuseColor.rgb.mul(radiosity.irradianceNode).div(Math.PI)

renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => {
  radiosity.update(renderer) // recomputes only when an input changed
  renderer.render(scene, camera)
})

To bounce only the direct light a self-shadow leaves, compose lightIrradiance() with its visibility:

import { storage } from 'three/tsl'

const visibility = storage(masks.visibility, 'vec4', masks.count).toReadOnly()
radiosity.irradiance = (position, normal, index) =>
  radiosity.lightIrradiance(keyLight)(position, normal).mul(visibility.element(index).x)

renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => {
  if (masks.update(renderer)) radiosity.needsUpdate = true // new visibility: the bounce reads it
  radiosity.update(renderer)
  renderer.render(scene, camera)
})

SelfShadowVisibilityMasks.guide:
import * as THREE from 'three/webgpu'
import { attribute } from 'three/tsl'
import { SelfShadowVisibilityMasks } from 'three-advanced-techniques'

// The mesh's geometry needs an index and normals; up to four lights of any kind
const masks = new SelfShadowVisibilityMasks(mesh, [keyLight, rimLight, sun, sky], { softness: 0.01 }) // σ in mesh units
await masks.bake(renderer, { resolution: 64 }) // kept as masks.data, plain typed arrays: cache them
// Optional: while a light moves in the mesh's frame, spread by one gather over pairs of vertices instead of the
// explicit steps; built in workers for that σ alone, structured-cloneable to cache
masks.motionKernel = await masks.diffusion.createKernel(masks.softness, { clusterSize: 2, mass: 0.99 })
await masks.compileAsync(renderer) // optional: every pipeline update() may build, ahead
mesh.geometry.setAttribute('visibility', masks.visibility) // per vertex: light 0's visibility in x, light 1's in y, …

// Each direct light's contribution × its visibility: the rect lights', and the directional, point and spot lights'
const selfShadow = attribute('visibility', 'vec4')
const visibleFrom = (light) => selfShadow[{ [keyLight.id]: 'x', [rimLight.id]: 'y', [sun.id]: 'z' }[light.id]].saturate()
class MaskedLighting extends THREE.PhysicalLightingModel {
  directRectArea(input, builder) {
    super.directRectArea({ ...input, lightColor: input.lightColor.mul(visibleFrom(input.lightNode.light)) }, builder)
  }
  direct(input, builder) {
    super.direct({ ...input, lightColor: input.lightColor.mul(visibleFrom(input.lightNode.light)) }, builder)
  }
}
mesh.material.setupLightingModel = () => new MaskedLighting()
// An ambient or hemisphere light's or a probe's visibility is the occlusion of that sky: it scales the indirect light
mesh.material.aoNode = selfShadow.w.saturate()

renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => {
  masks.update(renderer) // evaluates only the lights that moved in the mesh's frame
  renderer.render(scene, camera)
})

SSRNode.summary: Screen-space reflections by Newton's method on the G-buffer, in place of the scene's environment specular.
SSRNode.intro: Screen-space reflections by Newton's method on the G-buffer, in place of the scene's environment specular:
SSRNode.usage:
const scenePass = pass(scene, camera, { samples: 0 })
scenePass.setMRT(mrt({ output, velocity, ...ssrGBuffer() }))   // keep velocity RG16F

const reflections = ssr(color, scenePass, { roughnessCutoff: 0.6, thickness: 0.2 })

renderPipeline.outputNode = renderOutput(taauNode.getTextureNode())

NoodleSimulation.summary: Noodles, ropes and cables on the GPU.
NoodleSimulation.intro: Noodles, ropes and cables on the GPU: strands that bend, buckle, pile up and never pass through each other, drawn as one instanced tube:
NoodleSimulation.usage:
const noodles = new NoodleSimulation(curves, material, { radius: 0.05, particlesPerNoodle: 32 })
noodles.colliders.push(new THREE.Sphere(center, 0.5))
scene.add(noodles)
await noodles.compileAsync(renderer)
renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => {
  noodles.update(renderer, timer.getDelta())
  renderer.render(scene, camera)
})
const hit = await noodles.pickAsync(raycaster)
noodles.startGrab(hit.particle).moveGrab(hit.position)
NoodleSimulation.guide:
Each noodle is a chain of particles joined by capsules, simulated in small fixed time steps so it moves the same at any frame rate. After Macklin et al., XPBD: Position-Based Simulation of Compliant Constrained Dynamics (2016), Han and Harada, Tridiagonal Matrix Formulation for Inextensible Hair Strand Simulation (2013), Bergou et al., Discrete Elastic Rods (2008), Ericson, Real-Time Collision Detection (2005), Tonge et al., Mass Splitting for Jitter-Free Parallel Rigid Body Simulation (2012), Wu et al., A Safe and Fast Repulsion Method for GPU-based Cloth Self Collisions (2020), and Chen et al., Offset Geometric Contact (2025).

Usage

import * as THREE from 'three/webgpu'
import { NoodleSimulation } from 'three-advanced-techniques'

// one curve per noodle: its rest shape and starting pose
const curves = points.map((p) => new THREE.LineCurve3(p, p.clone().add(new THREE.Vector3(0, -3, 0))))
const noodles = new NoodleSimulation(curves, material, { radius: 0.05, particlesPerNoodle: 32 })
noodles.bendingCompliance = 0.5 // stiffer
noodles.bendingPlasticity = 0 // ropes and cables spring back
noodles.colliders.push(new THREE.Sphere(center, 0.5))
scene.add(noodles)

const timer = new THREE.Timer()
renderer.setAnimationLoop((time) => {
  timer.update(time)
  noodles.update(renderer, timer.getDelta())
  renderer.render(scene, camera)
})

How it works

  • Bending: each noodle bends like a soft rod, solved on the GPU one noodle per workgroup. bendingCompliance sets how floppy it is, whatever its particle count: 2 is cooked spaghetti, 0.08 a stiff rod. bendingPlasticity lets a noodle keep the shape it settles in; at 0 it springs back.
  • Length: each noodle's length is solved exactly in one step, so it never stretches. It squashes a little more easily, so a noodle landing on its end buckles.
  • Contacts: segments are sorted into a grid, so each one only tests its neighbours, and overlapping noodles are pushed apart with friction.
  • No passing through: with strictCollisions, a particle never moves more than about half its distance to the nearest other segment in one step, so noodles can't pass through each other.
  • Colliders: a ground plane plus planes, spheres, boxes and capsules you can move every frame. Add another NoodleSimulation to colliders and the two collide.
  • Drawing: every noodle is drawn as a tube in one draw call, with any material.
  • Extending it: extraPasses runs your own compute shaders on its data, and pickAsync, startGrab, moveGrab and endGrab let you drag a noodle.

WormSimulation.guide:
Worms are noodles that move themselves: they only add pushes and muscle bends, so the noodle physics, length, bending and collisions, always wins. Everything runs on the GPU, and nothing is read back to the CPU.

Usage

import * as THREE from 'three/webgpu'
import { WormSimulation } from 'three-advanced-techniques'
import { BodyField } from './BodyField.js' // copied from the repo's examples/utils, not in the package

const field = BodyField.fromSkinnedMesh(body) // the body the worms climb: round cones on its bones
const worms = new WormSimulation(curves, material, { field, radius: 0.024, particlesPerNoodle: 18 })
worms.colliders.push(...field.colliders)
scene.add(worms)

const timer = new THREE.Timer()
renderer.setAnimationLoop((time) => {
  timer.update(time)
  const dt = timer.getDelta()
  field.update(dt)
  worms.update(renderer, dt)
  renderer.render(scene, camera)
})

worms.poke(raycaster) // knock worms off along a ray

How it works

  • Crawling: muscles bend each worm in a travelling wave, like a snake. Worms also steer and squirm, and can squeeze along their length (peristalsis).
  • States: each worm is loose, crawling, climbing or held, and can switch once a frame.
  • Body: the worms climb a shape given as a distance field: how far each point is from its surface, which way is out, and how fast it moves. Inside it, worms are nearly weightless and fill it from the bottom up; those that don't fit drip off and crawl back.
  • Floor grip: worms stick to the floor and slide more easily forward than sideways, so the wave moves them forward.
  • Tools: poke, blast, strike and collapse knock worms off; pick, grabPicked and moveGrabAlongRay drag one; reset({ clock: true }) replays a run.

GPUTierDetector.summary: Picks a quality tier for the device at load.
GPUTierDetector.intro: Picks a quality tier for the device at load: a classification from the adapter's static signals (vendor, architecture, limits, navigator.userAgentData), then optionally a short GPU benchmark. Plain WebGPU, no three.js needed: it runs before any renderer exists, or reads one's.
GPUTierDetector.usage:
import { GPUTierDetector } from 'three-advanced-techniques/utils/GPUTierDetector.js'

const detector = new GPUTierDetector(['Low', 'Medium', 'High'], { caps: { mobile: 'Low', desktop: 'Medium' } })
const found = await detector.detect() // an adapter of its own, a few ms
// { tier: 'Low', level: 0, deviceClass: 'mobile', mobile: true, reasons: ['apple GPU on a mobile device'], … }
// or detect(renderer) after `await renderer.init()`, detect(device) or detect(adapter)

// optionally, time one unit of the app's GPU work (or omit it for a built-in reference set)
const timed = await detector.benchmark(renderer, () => app.simulate(renderer, 1 / 60))
// { tier: 'Medium', level: 1, ms: 11.4, samples: [11.2, 11.4, 11.9], roundTrip: 0.04, warmups: 3, … }
const capped = detector.tiers[Math.min(found.level, timed.level)]
GPUTierDetector.outro:
detect() sorts the device into a class, fallback, weak, mobile or desktop, and caps the tier at the class's highest (caps); its mobile is true for a phone or a tablet by navigator.userAgentData (mobile, or a formFactors hint of Mobile, Tablet, XR or Watch), else by the user-agent string and touch points (Safari, Firefox), or for a mobile vendor's GPU outside Windows (an Android tablet asking for desktop sites, a Chromebook), whatever the class.

benchmark() times workload as wall time from the call to device.queue.onSubmittedWorkDone(), minus an empty submit's round trip, and picks the highest tier whose threshold the median meets. Pass-timestamp sums are never used: on Vulkan a pass's begin stamp can absorb the wait for earlier work. Compile the workload's pipelines before benchmark(), or the warm-up run carries the compile. It times the whole device queue: stop anything else that submits while it runs (renderer.setAnimationLoop(null), or skip the loop's render), or its frames land in the samples. Without workload it times a built-in reference set of compute dispatches, on the given device or, with none, on a device of its own.
